text: This lesson covers working with ServiceNow Support — the vendor's own support channels, and how to use them well when a problem genuinely needs them.

Not every slowdown is ServiceNow's responsibility, and not every slowdown is something an admin can fix alone. A recursive Business Rule, an inefficient GlideRecord query, an unindexed custom table — these are problems the customer introduced through their own configuration, and they're the customer's own responsibility to fix, using the tools this course has built across five chapters: the Slow Request Log, the Script Performance Profiler, query plans, Instance Health. A genuine platform or infrastructure issue — something tied to the underlying hosting, a platform-level bug, an outage on the shared service — sits on ServiceNow's side of that line, and that's exactly what vendor support exists for. Lesson 19's triage work is what tells you which side of that line you're actually standing on.

A vague report like the instance feels slow, please investigate, is close to useless to Support — there's no transaction to pull up, no time window to search against, so the first reply is almost always a request for exactly the evidence that should have been gathered before the case was opened. What actually moves a case forward instead is concrete and timestamped: specific Slow Request Log entries, the exact start and end time, which users or features were affected, and what, if anything, changed recently.

That's the same evidence Lesson 19's triage sequence already produces: scope confirmed through Instance Health, timing checked against the deployment history, resource usage checked for exhaustion. A well-triaged incident essentially writes its own support case — when it happened, how it was confirmed, what's already been ruled out — handed over up front so ServiceNow's engineers can start investigating the actual mechanism immediately, instead of spending the first exchange just establishing what happened at all.

Gathering that evidence first isn't bureaucratic box-checking — it's the single thing that determines whether a case resolves in one exchange or ten. Next up: writing a real postmortem once a platform incident is actually resolved.
